blocks.text: A pharmacist is asked why a litre of 0.9% saline given to a dehydrated patient stays almost entirely outside the cells, while a litre of 5% glucose in water ends up mostly inside them. Both bags look like clear water. The difference comes from how body water is divided into compartments and from which solutes can pull water across cell membranes.

blocks.markdown: Water is the most abundant molecule in the body. **Total body water (TBW)** is roughly 60 per cent of body weight in an adult man and roughly 50 to 55 per cent in an adult woman, because fat contains little water and women on average carry proportionally more fat. TBW is also lower in obesity and in older adults and higher in infants. All figures here are typical approximations that vary between individuals.

blocks.title: Fluid compartments
blocks.text: Intracellular fluid (ICF) is the water inside cells, about two thirds of TBW. Extracellular fluid (ECF) is all water outside cells, about one third of TBW. The ECF has two main parts: plasma, the fluid component of blood inside the vessels, and interstitial fluid, the fluid bathing the cells outside the vessels. Plasma is separated from interstitial fluid by the capillary wall, and the ICF is separated from the interstitial fluid by the cell membrane.

headers: Volume in a 70 kg man (TBW 42 L)
blocks.caption: Approximate distribution of total body water in a 70 kg adult man. Plasma and interstitial fluid together make up the ECF.

blocks.markdown: Water crosses cell membranes freely by **osmosis**, moving from the side with lower solute concentration to the side with higher solute concentration until the effective osmotic concentrations match. Cell membranes are poorly permeable to sodium (it is pumped out by the sodium-potassium ATPase) but permeable to water, so sodium and its anions are the main particles that hold water in the ECF, while potassium and organic anions hold water inside cells. Under steady conditions the ICF and ECF have the same osmotic concentration.

blocks.title: Osmolarity and tonicity
blocks.text: Osmolarity is the number of osmotically active particles per litre of solution (mOsm/L); osmolality is the number per kilogram of water (mOsm/kg), and the two are numerically close in plasma. Tonicity describes the effect of a solution on cell volume: an isotonic solution leaves cell volume unchanged, a hypotonic solution makes cells swell, a hypertonic solution makes cells shrink. Only solutes that cannot freely cross the membrane (effective osmoles, such as sodium and glucose in the absence of insulin action) contribute to tonicity. Normal plasma osmolality is about 275 to 295 mOsm/kg, with the range varying by laboratory.

blocks.caption: Estimated plasma osmolarity. Sodium is doubled to account for its accompanying anions (mainly chloride and bicarbonate). All concentrations in mmol/L.

blocks.title: Calculating plasma osmolarity
blocks.prompt: A blood sample shows sodium 138 mmol/L, glucose 5 mmol/L and urea 6 mmol/L. Estimate the plasma osmolarity.

steps.text: Double the sodium concentration to include its anions: 2 x 138 = 276 mOsm/L.
Add the glucose and urea concentrations, each of which contributes one osmole per mole: 276 + 5 + 6.
Compare with the typical range of about 275 to 295 mOsm/kg: the value lies within it.

blocks.answer: Estimated plasma osmolarity is about 287 mOsm/L, within the normal range, so this is neither hypo- nor hyperosmolar.

blocks.title: Urea counts for osmolarity but not tonicity
blocks.text: Urea crosses cell membranes freely, so it adds to measured and calculated osmolarity but does not draw water out of cells and is therefore an ineffective osmole. Sodium is the dominant effective osmole of the ECF. Glucose is normally only about 5 mmol/L, but in uncontrolled hyperglycaemia it rises to tens of mmol/L and acts as an effective osmole, pulling water out of cells.

Isotonic in the bag, but the glucose is metabolised, leaving free water

Cells swell slightly as ECF osmolarity falls

Water moves from ICF into ECF
blocks.caption: Predicting the effect of infusion on compartments. Fluids are described here for physiology teaching, not as treatment guidance.

blocks.title: A hypotonic load
blocks.prompt: A 70 kg man (TBW 42 L, osmolality 290 mOsm/kg) takes in 1 L of solute-free water, none of which is excreted. Estimate how much water enters the ICF and what the final plasma osmolality will be.

steps.text: Free water distributes across the whole TBW, so each compartment receives a share proportional to its size: the ICF takes about two thirds and the ECF about one third.
The ECF receives the remaining 0.33 L, which dilutes its sodium and lowers ECF osmolality; water then moves into the cells until ICF and ECF osmolalities match.
The number of osmoles has not changed, but the water volume has: total osmoles 290 x 42 = 12 180 mOsm spread over 43 L.

blocks.answer: About 0.67 L enters the cells, the final osmolality is about 283 mOsm/kg, and the cells are slightly swollen.

items: Identify what is being added: salt-containing isotonic solution, free water, or a hypertonic solute.
Ask whether the solute can cross cell membranes. If it is confined to the ECF (sodium), the water it carries stays in the ECF.
If the added fluid has the same osmolarity as plasma, there is no osmotic gradient and no water moves between ECF and ICF.
If the ECF becomes hypotonic, water moves into cells; if hypertonic, water moves out of cells, until the osmolarities match.

blocks.title: Isotonic in the bag does not mean isotonic in the body
blocks.text: A 5% glucose solution is approximately isotonic in the bag, but it behaves as a hypotonic load once the glucose is taken up and metabolised. Do not treat it as an ECF replacement fluid. Likewise, calculated osmolarity can be misleading when sodium is low because of hyperglycaemia: glucose has drawn water out of cells and diluted the sodium.

points: TBW is about 60 per cent of body weight in men (about 50 to 55 per cent in women); two thirds is intracellular and one third extracellular, and the ECF is about one quarter plasma and three quarters interstitial fluid.
Plasma osmolarity is estimated as 2 x [Na+] + [glucose] + [urea] in mmol/L, with a normal range of about 275 to 295 mOsm/kg varying by laboratory.
Sodium is the main effective osmole of the ECF; urea is an ineffective osmole because it crosses membranes freely.
Isotonic saline expands only the ECF; free water (including glucose that is metabolised) distributes across all TBW and swells cells; hypertonic solutions shrink cells.

questions.stem: In a healthy adult, approximately what fraction of total body water lies inside cells?

options.text: About one quarter
About one third
About one half
About two thirds

distractorRationale.a: One quarter is closer to the fraction of the ECF that is plasma, not the ICF share of TBW.
distractorRationale.b: One third is the ECF share of TBW, so it is the wrong way round.
distractorRationale.c: One half is not a standard division of body water.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: ICF is about two thirds and ECF about one third of TBW.

questions.explanation: Roughly two thirds of body water is intracellular and one third extracellular. In a 70 kg man with 42 L of TBW this is about 28 L of ICF and 14 L of ECF.

questions.stem: A 75 kg man has total body water equal to 60 per cent of body weight. Assume the ECF is one third of TBW and his plasma volume is 3.0 L. What is the approximate volume of his interstitial fluid?

options.text: 9 L

distractorRationale.a: 15 L is the whole ECF; the plasma volume has not been subtracted.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: TBW 45 L, ECF 15 L, interstitial fluid 15 - 3 = 12 L.
distractorRationale.d: 9 L would follow from taking the ECF as only 12 L, which underestimates TBW or the ECF fraction.

questions.explanation: TBW is 0.6 x 75 = 45 L and the ECF is one third of this, 15 L. Interstitial fluid is the ECF minus plasma, 15 - 3 = 12 L.

questions.stem: A patient's blood results show sodium 142 mmol/L, glucose 6 mmol/L and urea 5 mmol/L. Using the estimate 2 x [Na+] + [glucose] + [urea], calculate the plasma osmolarity in mOsm/L.
questions.explanation: Doubling sodium gives 284 mOsm/L, and adding glucose (6) and urea (5) gives 284 + 6 + 5 = 295 mOsm/L. This sits at the upper end of the usual reference range, which varies by laboratory.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with thirst and polyuria. His blood tests show sodium 128 mmol/L, glucose 40 mmol/L and urea 10 mmol/L. Calculate his plasma osmolarity in mOsm/L using 2 x [Na+] + [glucose] + [urea].
questions.explanation: Doubling sodium gives 256, and adding glucose 40 and urea 10 gives 256 + 40 + 10 = 306 mOsm/L. Although sodium is low, the plasma is hyperosmolar because the high glucose is acting as an effective osmole, drawing water out of cells into the ECF and diluting the sodium.

questions.stem: A normally hydrated adult is given 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously. Once equilibrium is reached, which of the following is most likely?

options.text: The ECF volume rises by about 1 L and the ICF volume is essentially unchanged
The ICF volume rises by about 0.67 L and the ECF volume rises by about 0.33 L
The ICF volume falls as water moves into the ECF
The plasma volume rises by the full 1 L and the interstitial volume is unchanged

questions.correctOptionText: The ECF volume rises by about 1 L and the ICF volume is essentially unchanged

distractorRationale.a: Correct: isotonic saline adds no osmotic gradient, so the volume stays in the ECF.
distractorRationale.b: This is the distribution of free water, not of isotonic saline.
distractorRationale.c: Water would leave cells only if the ECF became hypertonic, which isotonic saline does not cause.
distractorRationale.d: Saline equilibrates across the capillary wall, so about three quarters ends up in the interstitial space.

questions.explanation: Isotonic saline has the same osmolarity as plasma, so there is no osmotic gradient across cell membranes and no water moves into or out of cells. The sodium is confined to the ECF, so the infused litre remains there, distributing between plasma and interstitial fluid.

questions.stem: A research volunteer is given a small volume of 3% sodium chloride (hypertonic saline) in a controlled study. Which change in compartment volumes would be predicted once equilibrium is reached?

options.text: ICF volume rises and ECF volume falls
ICF volume falls and ECF volume rises
Both ICF and ECF volumes fall
ICF volume is unchanged and ECF volume rises

questions.correctOptionText: ICF volume falls and ECF volume rises

distractorRationale.a: This is the response to a hypotonic load, the opposite direction.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the extra sodium raises ECF osmolarity, drawing water out of cells.
distractorRationale.c: A solute and water load increases total body water, so both compartments cannot fall.
distractorRationale.d: This describes isotonic saline; the hypertonic fluid creates an osmotic gradient across the cell membrane.

questions.explanation: Hypertonic saline raises the sodium, and hence the effective osmolarity, of the ECF. Water moves out of cells down its osmotic gradient until osmolarities match, so ICF shrinks and ECF expands by more than the volume infused.

questions.stem: A 50 kg woman has total body water equal to 55 per cent of body weight and a plasma osmolality of 290 mOsm/kg. She drinks 1.5 L of solute-free water, none of which is excreted and no solutes are lost. Assuming complete equilibration, calculate her final osmolality in mOsm/kg.
questions.explanation: TBW is 0.55 x 50 = 27.5 L and the total osmoles are 290 x 27.5 = 7975 mOsm, which do not change. Spread over 27.5 + 1.5 = 29.0 L the osmolality is 7975 / 29.0 = 275 mOsm/kg, showing how a hypotonic load dilutes all compartments and causes cells to swell slightly.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney failure has plasma urea of 40 mmol/L, with normal sodium and glucose. Which statement about the effect of this urea on cells is correct?

options.text: The high urea raises measured osmolarity and also draws water out of cells, shrinking them
The high urea raises measured osmolarity but, because urea crosses cell membranes freely, it does not cause a sustained shift of water out of cells
The high urea lowers plasma osmolarity because urea is a small molecule
The high urea has no effect on osmolarity because it is not an osmotically active particle

questions.correctOptionText: The high urea raises measured osmolarity but, because urea crosses cell membranes freely, it does not cause a sustained shift of water out of cells

distractorRationale.a: This treats urea as an effective osmole; it equilibrates across the membrane so produces no sustained gradient.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: urea contributes to osmolarity but is an ineffective osmole.
distractorRationale.c: Every dissolved particle adds to osmolarity; urea raises it.
distractorRationale.d: Urea is osmotically active and appears in the osmolarity formula; it simply does not determine tonicity.

questions.explanation: Osmolarity counts all dissolved particles, so urea adds its concentration to the total. Tonicity, however, depends only on solutes that cannot cross the membrane; because urea equilibrates across cell membranes, it does not hold water in the ECF or shift water out of cells.

questions.stem: A 70 kg man is given 1 L of 5% glucose in water intravenously. Describe how the water is distributed among the body fluid compartments after the glucose has been taken up and metabolised, and explain the direction of water movement between the ECF and ICF.
markingGuide: States that glucose is metabolised or taken into cells, leaving free water in effect
States that free water distributes across total body water in proportion to compartment size: about two thirds ICF and one third ECF
Gives approximate volumes, around 0.67 L into cells and 0.33 L into the ECF, with only a small fraction (about 0.07 L, roughly 70 mL) staying in plasma
Explains that the added water initially dilutes the ECF, lowering ECF osmolarity
Explains that water then moves by osmosis from the hypotonic ECF into cells until ICF and ECF osmolarities are equal
Concludes that cells swell slightly and that this fluid is a poor way to expand plasma volume
questions.explanation: Once the glucose is metabolised, the infusion is equivalent to free water, which is shared across ICF and ECF according to their sizes. Because the ECF is diluted first, water moves into cells by osmosis until osmolarity is equal everywhere, so only a small share of the litre (about 70 mL, since plasma is about 3 of the 42 L of body water) remains in the plasma.

questions.stem: Describe the distribution of total body water in a 70 kg adult man among the intracellular fluid, interstitial fluid and plasma, giving approximate volumes, and state which ions are the main cation in the ICF and in the ECF.
markingGuide: TBW about 60 per cent of body weight, so about 42 L
ICF about two thirds of TBW, about 28 L
ECF about one third of TBW, about 14 L
Plasma about 3 L and interstitial fluid about 11 L of the ECF
Main ICF cation is potassium; main ECF cation is sodium
Notes that the cell membrane separates ICF from interstitial fluid and the capillary wall separates plasma from interstitial fluid
questions.explanation: TBW of about 42 L divides into roughly 28 L of ICF and 14 L of ECF, and the ECF is itself divided into about 3 L plasma and 11 L interstitial fluid. Potassium dominates inside cells and sodium outside because of the sodium-potassium ATPase, and these gradients are what makes sodium the principal effective osmole of the ECF.
